claims.text: The studied material is an as-solidified, Co-free, equiatomic FeNiCrMn alloy.
Dynamic mechanical behavior across temperature and strain-rate regimes is governed by a transition between thermally activated dislocation mobility and deformation twinning.
At higher temperatures and lower strain rates, enhanced dislocation glide dominates deformation.
At lower temperatures and higher strain rates, limited thermal activation promotes deformation twinning.
Deformation twinning contributes to the strength-ductility balance of FeNiCrMn.
Temperature and strain rate produce quantitative changes in dislocation density and twin-boundary density.
At high temperatures and low strain rates, thermal activation promotes dislocation glide and recovery.
At cryogenic temperatures or high strain rates, reduced dislocation mobility forces deformation to be accommodated by twinning.
Twinning preserves ductility despite an increase in strength.
Elevated-temperature, low-strain-rate tests will show lower yield strength and minimal twinning.
Lower-temperature, higher-strain-rate tests will show increased yield strength, increased strain hardening, and a higher density of deformation twins.
Changes in twin density and dislocation structure will correlate with shifts in the stress-strain response.
At room temperature and static or moderate strain rates, dislocation glide primarily governs deformation and relatively few twins occur.
Post-solidification processing can introduce precipitates or altered defect states that fundamentally change the deformation behavior.
Grain size or short-range order may modify the predicted temperature- and strain-rate-dependent behavior.
A controlled matrix of temperature and strain-rate tests on as-solidified samples, followed by TEM and EBSD, can test the proposed mechanism.
Failure to observe a systematic increase in twinning at low temperature and high strain rate, or observation of an unchanged dominant mechanism across conditions, would falsify the hypothesis.
